questions.stem_markdown:
The engine of a motorcycle can generate a maximum power of 105 kW. The mass of the motorcycle and its rider is 400 kg. The total resistance to the motion of the motorcycle and its rider is $cv$ N, where $v\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ is the motorcyclist's speed and $c$ is a constant.

The motorcyclist travels along a straight horizontal road under maximum engine power. When the motorcyclist's speed is $35\,\text{m s}^{-1}$, his acceleration is $0.5\,\text{m s}^{-2}$.

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Use of N2L; allow sign errors but must be 3 terms. Allow $$F$$ or any non-zero value for the driving force (but not 105000). If assuming $$a = 0$$ then e.g. $$105000 = c \times 35^2$$ ($$\Rightarrow c = 85.714...$$) scores **B1 M0**.
**AG** – a correct equation for $$c$$ e.g. $$3000 - 35 \times c = 400 \times 0.5$$ followed by $$c = 80$$ scores **A1**.
**B1** for correct weight component: $$\pm 400g \times \frac{3}{20}$$ or $$\pm 400g \times \sin\left(\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{20}\right)\right)$$. $$[= \pm 600]$$.

OE. **M1** for applying N2L with the correct number of dimensionally correct terms (with $$a = 0$$) **leading to a three term quadratic equation/expression in $$v$$**. Allow sign errors and sin/cos mix on the weight component. **Must** be using $$c = 80$$ for this mark.
CWO. Allow exact $$\frac{-15 + 5\sqrt{849}}{4}$$ or AWRT 32.7. (For reference: 32.6720057...). If negative value ($$-40.172...$$) stated, then must be rejected for this mark.

parts.prompt_markdown: Find the work done against friction in moving the block from A to B.
Use an energy method to find the speed of the block at B.

skills: Calculate friction force from normal reaction
Compute work done against friction over a displacement
Use an energy balance to determine speed at a new position
methods: Work against friction = friction force × distance
Energy conservation with work by non-conservative forces included

questions.stem_markdown:
A block of mass 4 kg is pulled along a rough horizontal road by a constant force of magnitude 25 N acting at an angle of $36^\circ$ above the horizontal. The block moves in a straight line passing through two points A and B on the road, where $AB = 120$ m. The coefficient of friction between the block and the road is 0.4.

The speed of the block at A is $7\,\text{m s}^{-1}$.

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Attempt to resolve vertically to form an equation for the normal contact force for the block; correct number of dimensionally correct terms, condone sign errors, and sin/cos mix on the 25 N force term. Use of $$R = 4g$$ scores no marks in this part.

Use of Work done $$= 0.4R \times 120$$ ONLY so M0 if subtracting/adding the Work done by the pulling force to this value e.g. a final answer of 1212 (or 1210) coming from $$120 \times (25\cos 36 - 0.4 \times (40 - 25\sin 36))$$ scores M1 M0 A0.
CWO 1210 or final AWRT 1215 or 1214 (usually coming from using $$R = 25.3$$). For reference: 1214.6576...
SOI, by KE terms on opposite sides of an equation with the same sign so must imply a change in KE (e.g. $$2v^2$$ on one side and 98 on the other).

Attempt at work-energy equation using their work done against friction from **3(a)** with four dimensionally correct terms but allow sign errors and sin/cos mix on the pulling force term. Dependent on **both M1** marks in **3(a)** unless the total work done is recovered in this part e.g. a candidate might, in **3(a)**, find the total work done by the block (which if correct is 1212.39...) rather than the required work done against friction. Therefore, an answer of 1212.39... **3(a)** would score **M1 M0 A0** but then seeing $$2v^2 - 98 = 1212.39\dots$$ (or even 1210 but only if coming from 1212.39...) followed by 25.6 would score full marks in this part. **M0** if using $$25 \times 120$$ for the pulling force.
AWRT 25.6. (For reference: 25.59680...).
This is for getting $$a = 2.53$$. (For reference: $$a = 2.525819\dots$$).
AWRT 25.6. (For reference: 25.59680...).

parts.prompt_markdown: Find the value of $s$ when P has its minimum velocity, and find also the speed of P at this instant.
Find the acceleration of P at the instant when the direction of motion of P changes.

a = d2s/dt2

Use v = 0 to locate direction change

questions.stem_markdown: A particle P moves in a straight line. At time $t$ s after passing through a point O on the line, the displacement of P from O is $s$ m, where $s = 0.01t^3 - 0.3t^2 - 2.07t$.

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Decrease power by 1 and change of coefficient on the same term; $$a = \frac{v}{t}$$ is M0.
Allow un-simplified.

Allow un-simplified. Must follow from the correct **3 term quadratic** in $$t$$ for $$v$$ so A0 if coming from $$v = 0.03t^2 - 0.6t$$. Or the correct completing the square form for the correct expression for $$v$$.

Setting their $$a = 0$$ where $$a$$ is a two-term linear expression (of the form $$k_1t + k_2$$ where $$k_1, k_2 \neq 0$$) in $$t$$. Or setting their $$t - 10$$ (from completing the square on a three term quadratic in $$t$$) equal to 0.
CWO (so first four marks must have been awarded). Must be negative so do not allow $$s = -40.7 \Rightarrow s = 40.7$$ so no ISW. Saying that $$s = -40.7$$ or $$40.7$$ is A0.

CWO (so first four marks must have been awarded or first three marks if completing the square). Must be positive – allow A1 if negative sign is dropped without justification but saying speed is either $$-5.07$$ or $$5.07$$ is A0.
Set their 3 term quadratic expression in $$t$$ for $$v$$ equal to zero – dependent on first M1 mark in 4(a). This mark can be implied by a correct value of $$t = 23$$ appearing in this part.
CWO Ignore mention of $$t = -3$$. Working might appear in 4(a), but this value must be stated in 4(b) to earn this mark.
Their positive $$t$$ substituted into their two-term linear expression for $$a$$ – this mark can be implied by a correct answer.
OE e.g. $$\frac{39}{50}$$, etc. if $$-0.78$$ found then must be explicitly rejected.

questions.stem_markdown: Particles A and B, of masses 2 kg and 6 kg respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string. The string passes over a smooth fixed pulley and the particles hang vertically below the pulley. Both particles are initially held at rest at a height of 3.2 m above horizontal ground (see diagram). Particle A is projected vertically downwards with a speed of $1.2\,\text{m s}^{-1}$.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Attempt at N2L for either *A* or *B* or the system
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Correct number of dimensionally correct terms, allow sign errors. Condone using *a* = ±10 (or another incorrect value of *a*) in either the equation for *A* or *B* for this mark **only**.

For any two correct equations in *a* and *T* (or implied by correct answers) – note that *T* must be positive in one equation and negative in the other. Note that the three equations: 2*g* − *T* = 2*a*, *T* − 6*g* = 6*a* and 2*g* − 6*g* = 8*a* score **M1 A1** and lead to *T* = 3*g* and *a* = −0.5*g*.
From two N2L equations (both containing *a*) with the correct number of dimensionally correct terms OE.
*a***must** be positive – allow those who say *a* = −0.5*g* ⇒ *a* = 0.5*g* (or *a* = −5 ⇒ *a* = 5) without justification (but must be from correct working).

Using $$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$$ with $$s = \pm 3.2$$, $$u = \pm 1.2$$ and their $$a$$ from **5(a)** (not $$\pm g$$ but allow $$\pm 10$$ if come from wrong working in **5(a)**) – dependent on either a system equation with the correct number of dimensionally correct terms from **5(a)** or from equations for $$A$$ and $$B$$ that both contain the correct number of dimensionally correct terms – or other complete method to find $$t$$.
AWRT 1.4 or $$\frac{6 + 2\sqrt{209}}{25}$$. (For reference: 1.39654...).

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Distance $$A$$ travels from initial position to first time at rest: $$0 = 1.2^2 + 2 \times (-5) \times s_1 \quad (\Rightarrow s_1 = 0.144)$$ OR $$0 = (-1.2)^2 + 2 \times (5) \times s_1 \quad (\Rightarrow s_1 = -0.144)$$ OR $$s_1 = 1.2 \times 0.24 + \frac{1}{2} \times (-5) \times 0.24^2 \quad (\Rightarrow s_1 = 0.144)$$
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Attempt at finding the distance of $$A$$ below its starting position when it first comes to instantaneous rest. Using 1.2 and their 5 from **5(a)** – same dependency as in **5(b)** for the value of $$a$$ from **5(a)**. If using $$s = 1.2 \times t_1 + 0.5at_1^2$$ then their $$t_1$$ must have come from $$0 = 1.2 + a \times t_1$$ with their value of $$a$$ from **5(a)**. Energy for $$A$$: $$0 - \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 1.2^2 = 2 \times 10 \times s_1 - 30 \times s_1$$. Energy for $$B$$: $$0 - \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 1.2^2 = -6 \times 10 \times s_1 + 30 \times s_1$$. Energy for system: . $$0 - \left( \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 1.2^2 + \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 1.2^2 \right) = 2 \times 10 \times s_1 - 6 \times 10 \times s_1$$. If using energy – must have the correct number of dimensionally correct terms but allow sign errors. If considering either $$A$$ or $$B$$ then their value of $$T (= 30)$$ is dependent on both **M1** marks in **5(a)**.

Correct method to find the speed or speed² of A/B after travelling 3.2 metres (oe) – using 1.2 and their a from 5(a) – same dependency as in part (b) for the value of a from 5(a). If using $$v = u + at$$ then t must come from considering $$t_2 - t_1$$ (see reference on previous page).

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Distance A travels from a point 6.4 metres above the ground to rest: $$0 = 33.44 + 2 \times (-10) \times s_2 \quad (\Rightarrow s_2 = 1.672)$$
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Attempt to find the distance travelled by A after B hits the ground, using their w, a = -g and v = 0.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: Difference in distances is $$s_1 + 3.2 + s_2 = 5.016$$ m
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: AWRT 5.02 or 5.01 CWO.

parts.prompt_markdown: Find, in terms of $m$ and $u$, an expression for the velocity of Q after the collision and hence show that $m > 4.5$.

Q subsequently hits a vertical wall which is perpendicular to the direction of motion of Q. The speed of Q after the impact with the wall is a quarter of its speed before the impact with the wall. There are no further collisions between P and Q.

Given that $m$ is an integer, determine the largest possible value of $m$.

skills: Apply conservation of momentum for a 1D collision with direction reversal
Use given post-collision speed to determine another velocity in terms of m and u
Model the wall impact using the given speed ratio and determine constraints on m
methods: 1D momentum conservation using signed velocities
Use change of speed condition from wall impact (factor of 1/4)
Solve inequalities to identify the largest integer m
subtopics: Conservation of momentum in a collision
Reversal of directions and sign convention
Relating speed change of one mass after collision

questions.stem_markdown: Particle P of mass $m$ kg and particle Q of mass 2 kg are free to move on a smooth horizontal plane. P and Q are moving directly towards each other with speeds $u\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $3u\,\text{m s}^{-1}$ respectively. P and Q collide and the direction of motion of each particle is reversed by the collision. Immediately after the collision the speed of P is $\frac{u}{3}\,\text{m s}^{-1}$.

mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Attempt at conservation of momentum with correct number of terms. **Allow sign errors ONLY** so **no** misreads in this part. However, if using *g* with either (or both) masses, then allow this mark but do not allow subsequent **A** marks.
A correct (un-simplified) expression for the velocity of *Q* after the collision e.g. $$\frac{(2m-9)u}{3}, \frac{4}{6}mu - 3u,$$ $$\frac{mu - 6u + \frac{1}{3}mu}{2}$$, etc.

**AG CWO** – accept a correct expression for *v* put > 0 followed by *m* > 4.5. Note that $$\frac{2}{3}mu - 3u = 0 \Rightarrow m = 4.5 \therefore m > 4.5$$ is **A0**. Using trial and improvement to show that *v* is negative with value(s) of *m* that are less than 4.5 is **A0** unless they also show that *v* = 0 when *m* = 4.5. Similarly, if attempting to show that *v* is positive with value(s) of *m* that are greater than 4.5 they must also show that *v* = 0 when *m* = 4.5 for **A1**. This **A1** mark is dependent on the previous **A1** mark.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: [Q's speed is reduced by 75% by its impact with the wall ⇒] speed after impact is $$\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{2}{3}mu - 3u\right)\left[=\frac{1}{6}mu - \frac{3}{4}u\right]$$
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Follow through their v of the form $$k_1mu + k_2u$$ (if simplified) for $$k_1, k_2 \neq 0$$ from 6(a) OE e.g. $$\frac{(2m-9)u}{12}$$ or possibly implied by later working e.g. $$-\frac{1}{3}u \leqslant \frac{(9-2m)u}{12}$$. Allow ± e.g. $$-\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{2}{3}mu - 3u\right)$$. **Look out for this expression embedded in later (possibly incorrect) working.**

For $$\frac{1}{3}u \geqslant \frac{1}{4}v$$ with v of the form $$k_1mu + k_2u$$ for $$k_1, k_2 \neq 0$$ from 6(a) – allow > or = for this mark Note that $$\frac{4}{3}u = \frac{2}{3}mu - 3u$$ (which leads to m = 6.5) scores B1 M1 ONLY.
Solve to obtain an inequality of the form 'm <' or 'm ≤'. **Dependent on both previous marks - M0** if an equation for m found rather than an inequality for a range of values of m.
CWO – condone m = 6 from m < 6.5.

assets.description: Mechanics diagram showing a particle P on an inclined rough plane, with a horizontal force of 12 N acting on P in the vertical plane containing the line of greatest slope. The plane is inclined at angle theta to the horizontal.

relationships: The plane is inclined at an acute angle theta.
Friction acts between P and the plane.

skills: Write equilibrium equations along and perpendicular to the plane
Express friction force using normal reaction and coefficient of friction
Solve for the range of angles consistent with impending motion down the plane
methods: Set net force along plane to zero at impending equilibrium
Use R = mg cosθ and friction = μR
Use condition for impending sliding (limiting friction) to solve for μ and then θ
subtopics: Rough plane friction as function of normal reaction
Resolve forces along plane and normal direction
Determine friction coefficient and allowable angle range

questions.stem_markdown:
A particle P of mass 6 kg lies on a rough plane inclined at an acute angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. A horizontal force of magnitude 12 N acts on P as shown in the diagram. The line of action of this horizontal force lies in a vertical plane which contains the line of greatest slope of the plane that passes through P. The coefficient of friction between P and the plane is $\mu$.

P is in equilibrium and on the point of sliding down the plane.

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: For resolving in any direction to form an equation
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: Correct number of relevant dimensionally correct terms; allow sin/cos mix; allow sign errors. Forces that need resolving should be resolved, forces that do not need resolving should not be resolved.
Or $$12 + F \cos \theta = R \sin \theta$$ (resolving horizontally).
Or $$R \cos \theta + F \sin \theta = 6g$$ (resolving vertically).

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: For use of $$F = \mu R$$ to get an equation in $$\mu$$ and $$\theta$$ only
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: From dimensionally correct equations with the correct number of relevant terms (forces that need resolving should be resolved, forces that do not need resolving should not).

mark_scheme_items.content_markdown: $$6g \sin \theta - 12 \cos \theta = \mu(6g \cos \theta + 12 \sin \theta)$$ leading to $$\mu = \frac{5 \tan \theta - 1}{5 + \tan \theta}$$ With some evidence of intermediate step e.g. $$\frac{12 \cos \theta \left( \frac{5 \sin \theta}{\cos \theta} - 1 \right)}{12 \cos \theta \left( 5 + \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} \right)}$$ OR $$\frac{12 \cos \theta (5 \tan \theta - 1)}{12 \cos \theta (5 + \tan \theta)}$$ OR ‘divide by cosine’ OR use/mention of $$\tan \theta = \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}$$ OR $$\sin \theta = \tan \theta \cos \theta$$, etc.
mark_scheme_items.guidance_markdown: AG – CWO must give some indication of how the equation in sin/cos leads to the given answer e.g. $$\mu = \frac{6g \sin \theta - 12 \cos \theta}{6g \cos \theta + 12 \sin \theta}$$ then ‘divide through by cos’ gives $$\mu = \frac{5 \tan \theta - 1}{5 + \tan \theta}$$ scores A1 (so therefore mentioning ‘dividing by cos’). Seeing $$\mu = \frac{6g \sin \theta - 12 \cos \theta}{6g \cos \theta + 12 \sin \theta} = \frac{5 \tan \theta - 1}{5 + \tan \theta}$$ only is A0.

Set the numerator of $$\mu$$ either =, > or $$\geqslant$$ to 0 and obtain $$\tan \theta \sqcup k$$ where $$\sqcup$$ is =, > or $$\geqslant$$ and $$k \neq 0$$ - ignore any consideration of an upper bound (e.g. saying that $$\mu < 1$$).
AWRT 11.3 (11.30993...). Must be strict inequality. Allow $$\theta > 0.197(39...)$$ - if anything other than < 90 then **A0**.
